course.title: Calculus: Change and Accumulation
course.description: Bring points together, trace a tangent and build an area. Discover how change accumulates.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with algebra, function notation, powers and coordinate graphs. This introductory course develops polynomial limits, rates and accumulation.

paragraphs: Calculus is the mathematics of change. It answers two questions that algebra alone cannot. One is how fast something is changing at one exact moment. The other is how much has built up after a stretch of change. Engineers use it to design bridges and engines, scientists to model motion, growth and heat, and economists to study how costs and profits shift. Anyone who wants to read physics, statistics or machine learning in depth meets it early.

The course has 12 lessons in four parts. Approach a point looks at limits, continuity and the first derivative, by creeping up on a gap in a graph and watching where it heads. Work with rates gives the rules for finding slopes quickly, including the chain rule, and applies them to motion. Reverse and refine finds where curves turn, undoes a derivative and builds an area from thin strips. Follow accumulation gives areas a sign and shows that areas and slopes are two views of one idea.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, so a question comes only after you have been shown what it needs.
outcomes: You'll be able to find a limit by simplifying a fraction, and say when a graph has a break.
You'll be able to find the slope of a curve at a point, from a limit and with the power and chain rules.
You'll be able to read speed and acceleration from a position, and find where a curve turns.
You'll be able to estimate an area with rectangles and find it exactly with an antiderivative.
You'll be able to explain how the fundamental theorem links rates to totals, and use it to find net change.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with algebra, function notation, powers and graphs on coordinate axes.

lessons.title: Approaching a value

lead.text: Start on the left of the gap and take small steps towards x = 2. At x = 1.5 the fraction gives 3.5. At x = 1.9 it gives 3.9, and at x = 1.99 it gives 3.99. Each step takes us closer to 2, and each answer rises a little to meet the last.

Now come in from the right. At x = 2.5 the fraction gives 4.5, at x = 2.1 it gives 4.1 and at x = 2.01 it gives 4.01. These answers fall, and they settle at the place the left-hand answers were rising towards.

afterFigure.text: Neither walk ever reaches x = 2, and neither is allowed to. Yet the answers from both sides crowd in on 4, as though the graph were heading for a point at height 4 and only that point were missing. The next screen gives this behaviour a name.

lead.text: The number that the outputs crowd in on is called the limit. For our fraction, the limit as x approaches 2 is 4. Here approaching means that x gets as close to 2 as you like without ever being 2.

A graph does not need a gap for this to make sense. Take h(x) = 10 − x and let x creep up on 4. At 4.1 the output is 5.9, at 4.01 it is 5.99 and at 4.001 it is 5.999. The outputs close in on 6, so the limit of h(x) as x approaches 4 is 6. Mathematicians write that in a compact form.

afterFigure.text: Use the buttons under the picture to switch between the two graphs, and drag the slider to bring a dot in from each side. Both dots close in on the same height, and the picture reports it as the limit. The gap graph is drawn as x + 2, which is what our fraction equals at every input except 2. A later screen shows why.
A limit belongs to the nearby values. What the graph does at the point itself plays no part in it.

lead.text: Reading a limit from a list of numbers works the same way every time. Here are the outputs of a new function.

reveal.text: You looked at where the outputs were heading and ignored where they started. That is all it takes to read a limit from a list.

lead.text: Here is a second fraction with a gap, this time at x = 3, for the same reason as the first. Try an input just to the right of the gap.

reveal.text: 6.1 is one step on the way in from the right. The next screens find where the whole run of answers ends up.

lead.text: Walking up to a gap shows roughly where a graph is heading, and it needs a calculator. Algebra gives the answer exactly. The plan is to rewrite the fraction in a simpler form that agrees with it everywhere except at the gap.

Take (x² − x) ÷ x, which gives 0 ÷ 0 at x = 0. The top factors as x(x − 1). For any x other than 0 we can divide top and bottom by x, and the fraction becomes x − 1. Near 0 the fraction and x − 1 give the same answers, so the fraction is heading for 0 − 1 = −1.

Dividing by x is allowed because a limit only looks at inputs close to 0, never at 0 itself, so x is never zero when we do it. A result of 0 ÷ 0 is called an indeterminate form. The substitution told you nothing about the limit, so the next job is to simplify and look again.
Many gaps come from a difference of squares, where x² − a² = (x − a)(x + a). For example, x² − 100 = (x − 10)(x + 10).

steps.headline: Find the limit of (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x approaches 2.

workedSteps.text: Putting in x = 2 gives 0 ÷ 0, which settles nothing.
Factor the top as a difference of squares.
Cancel x − 2. Near 2 it is never zero.
Let x approach 2.

steps.headline: Find the limit of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) as x approaches 3.

workedSteps.text: Factor the top as (x − 3)(x + 3).
Cancel x − 3, which is allowed because x is never 3 nearby.
Let x approach 3.

steps.headline: The value in the gap doesn't matter

lead.text: So far every gap has been empty. Suppose someone fills it with a number of their choice. Take f(x) = x + 4 for every x except 1, and declare that f(1) = 0. The graph is the straight line x + 4 with one dot knocked down to height 0 above x = 1.

Walk in from either side and the outputs still crowd in on 5, because every point near x = 1 sits on the line. The odd dot at 0 is never part of the walk, since we never stand on x = 1. The limit is 5 and the assigned value is 0, so the two need not match.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the two pictures. Moving the dot changes nothing about where the line is heading. A limit follows the neighbours of a point. The value at the point is a separate fact that may agree with the limit or may not exist at all, and the next lesson looks at when they agree.

lead.text: Here the value at x = 2 has been set by hand, and the graph on either side of it is a straight line.

reveal.text: Moving one point did not move the line around it. A limit follows the neighbours, not the value assigned at the point.

lead.text: Same shape, new numbers: a quotient that gives 0 ÷ 0 at x = 4.

reveal.text: You cancelled the factor that caused the 0 ÷ 0, then let x approach 4. The limit exists even though the quotient is undefined at 4.

lessons.orientation: Separate the value approached near a point from the value assigned at the point.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Ask a calculator for (x² − 4) ÷ (x − 2) at x = 2 and it refuses. The top is 2² − 4, which is 0, and the bottom is 2 − 2, which is also 0. A zero divided by a zero has no answer.
Every other input works without trouble. Put in 3 and you get 5, and 2.5 gives 4.5. Draw all the answers and you have a smooth path with a single missing point, like one plank gone from a bridge.

You can't stand on the missing plank, but you can stand beside it. This lesson walks up to the gap from both sides to see where the graph is heading. It then finds that place exactly, without a calculator, and shows why the value at the gap itself makes no difference.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a limit by cancelling a common factor, and say why the value at the point itself doesn't matter.
intro.whyItMatters: Every derivative is a limit of this shape, where the quotient is undefined at the point.

recap.keyIdea: A limit is where the outputs head as the input closes in. It ignores the value at the point itself, so a 0 ÷ 0 gap is settled by simplifying nearby.

blocks.text: Back at the missing plank, you found where (x² − 4) ÷ (x − 2) is heading, and you learned to cancel the factor that causes the 0 ÷ 0 so that the answer comes out exactly. You also saw that a value placed in the gap by hand does not move the limit.

recap.nextHook: So far both sides of a gap have headed for the same height. A price list with a step in it is a place where they can disagree, and the next lesson starts at a shop till.

lessons.title: Both sides of a point

lead.text: Last lesson a point could be approached from anywhere, and the outputs always closed in on the same height. Often it matters which side you come from. Left means inputs smaller than the point, and right means inputs larger. On a graph, left is the side towards the negative end of the x-axis.

A car park shows the difference. It charges £1.50 for a stay under an hour and £4.50 for a stay of an hour or more. Let the stay creep up on one hour from below, at 50 minutes and then at 59 minutes 59 seconds, and the charge stays at £1.50. That steady value is the left-hand limit of the charge at one hour.

lead.text: Back at the shop, the basket total creeps up towards £20 from below.

reveal.text: Every basket just under £20 pays £3, so £3 is the left-hand limit at £20. Coming down from above, the fee is £7.

lead.text: With a name for each side, we can ask whether they match. Take a graph with a step in it, where the output is 1 for every input below 0 and −2 for every input of 0 or above. Coming from the left the outputs stay at 1, so the left-hand limit at 0 is 1. Coming from the right they stay at −2, so the right-hand limit is −2.

Those two numbers differ, so there is no single height that the graph heads for at 0. The two-sided limit, the ordinary limit of the last lesson, exists only when the left-hand and right-hand limits are the same number. When they differ, the two-sided limit does not exist.

afterFigure.text: Switch to the second picture, where both sides head for 3. There the two-sided limit exists and equals 3. The sides are never averaged. A jump from 1 down to −2 has no limit of −0.5 in the middle, because no output on either side is anywhere near that.

lead.text: Here is a function that jumps at 0. Follow its graph in towards 0 from the left.

reveal.text: Coming from the left you stayed on one level. What the function does at 0 itself, or on the right, does not change it.

lead.text: Same function. This time follow the graph in towards 0 from the right.

reveal.text: Left and right gave different numbers. The graph jumps at 0, so the two sides do not meet.

lead.text: A two-sided limit says where a graph is heading. A separate question is whether the graph actually arrives there. Take the line y = x + 1. At x = 3 it heads for 4, and its value there is 4, so the graph passes through the place it was heading for. A function that does this at a point is continuous there.

Continuity at a point needs the function to have a value there. It also needs the two-sided limit to exist, and the two numbers to be equal. Roughly, you can draw the graph through that point without lifting the pen.
A gap with no value fails the first condition and a jump fails the second. A dot that sits off the line, with both sides agreeing on a different height, fails the last.

steps.headline: Is f continuous at 2, where f(x) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2 and f(2) = 7?

workedSteps.text: From the left, x + 2 heads for 4. From the right, it also heads for 4.
The sides agree, so the two-sided limit is 4.
Compare with the value at the point.
The limit and the value differ, so f is not continuous at 2.

lead.text: Another function, the same three conditions. Look at the graph, then decide.

reveal.text: Each condition has to hold. Here the limit existed and the value existed, but they were not the same number.

lead.text: Sometimes a graph fails to be continuous only because one point is missing or misplaced, while the line around it is perfectly regular. Such a break can be repaired. The value to put in the gap is the number the neighbours are heading for.

Suppose g(x) = 3x + 1 for every x except 2, and g(2) is not defined. Both sides head for 3 × 2 + 1 = 7. Give g(2) the value 7 and all three conditions hold, because the value now exists and equals the two-sided limit. The graph is now continuous at 2.

afterFigure.text: A jump cannot be repaired this way. Whatever value you put at the break, one of the two sides still heads for a different number. Switch to the second picture to see why.

lead.text: A graph has one missing point at x = 2. The line 2x + 4 runs through everything around it. You choose what goes in the gap.

reveal.text: Your value had to match what the neighbours head for: 2 × 2 + 4. That is how a single missing point is repaired.

lessons.orientation: Use one-sided limits and the value at the point to decide continuity.

blocks.text: A shop charges £3 delivery on orders under £20 and £7 on orders of £20 or more. Your basket stands at £19.99, so delivery is £3. One more penny takes the total to £20.00, and the fee jumps to £7. Take the penny out and it falls back.

In the last lesson the outputs closed in on the same height from both sides. The fee behaves differently. What it heads for depends on whether the basket creeps up on £20 from below or comes down on it from above.

That raises a puzzle about when a limit exists at all. This lesson gives each direction a name, says what has to happen for the two to agree, and uses that to define what it means for a graph to have no break.

lessons.title: From average rate to instant rate

lead.text: A rate compares two changes. A tank holds 20 litres at the 2 minute mark and 50 litres at the 5 minute mark. The contents rose by 30 litres while the time rose by 3 minutes, so on average the tank filled at 30 ÷ 3 = 10 litres per minute.

Every average rate has this shape: the change in the output divided by the change in the input. It describes the whole stretch. The tank may have filled quickly at first and slowly later, and the average hides that.
Here f(a) and f(b) are the outputs at the start and end of the stretch, and b − a is its length. We write f for any function, and a and b for two chosen inputs.

lead.text: Back to the odometer from the start of the lesson.

reveal.text: You divided the change in distance by the change in time. That is an average rate, and it says nothing about any single moment.

lead.text: The same idea works on a graph. Take the curve y = x² and pick two points on it, at x = 0 and x = 2. The heights are 0 and 4, so the average rate between them is (4 − 0) ÷ (2 − 0) = 2. That number is also the slope of the straight line through the two points, because the rise is 4 and the run is 2.
A line drawn through two points of a curve is called a secant. Its slope is the average rate over the stretch between the points, and a steep secant means the curve climbs quickly over that stretch.

afterFigure.text: Use the buttons to compare a wide stretch with a narrower one, and drag the slider to shrink the stretch. The secant turns as its second point slides towards the first, and the slope reported under the picture changes with it. Keep an eye on that turning, because the rest of the lesson builds on it.

lead.text: Work out an average rate on the same curve, this time between x = 1 and x = 3.

reveal.text: You divided the change in height by the change in input. That is the slope of the secant, and it belongs to the whole stretch.

lead.text: To get the rate at one point, say x = 1 on y = x², we need a second point to draw the secant through, and then we move it closer. Call the second point 1 + h, where h is the width of the stretch. The height at x = 1 is 1.

Try some widths. With h = 1 the slope is (4 − 1) ÷ 1 = 3. Halve the width to h = 0.5 and it becomes (2.25 − 1) ÷ 0.5 = 2.5. At h = 0.1 it is (1.21 − 1) ÷ 0.1 = 2.1. The slopes fall towards 2 as the stretch shrinks.

afterFigure.text: We cannot set h = 0 to get the slope exactly, because that would be 0 ÷ 0, the same trouble as the gap in the first lesson. The way out is the same too. The slope at the point is the limit of the secant slopes as h approaches 0, and a limit never needs h to be 0.

steps.headline: Find the slope of the secant for f(x) = x² from x = 1 to x = 1 + h, as h approaches 0.

workedSteps.text: Write the secant slope.
Expand the top.
Divide by h. Allowed, because h is never zero.
Let h approach 0.

steps.headline: Find the slope of the secant for f(x) = x² from x = 2 to x = 2 + h, as h approaches 0.

workedSteps.text: Expand the top.
Divide by h, for h ≠ 0.
Let h approach 0.

lead.text: The worked lines show the pattern. The h that gets in the way vanishes as h shrinks, and what remains is the limit of the secant slopes. At x = 1 it was 2, and at x = 2 it was 4.

That limit is the derivative of the function at the point, written f′(a) for the point x = a. It is the instantaneous rate of change, the rate at that single instant. On the graph it is the slope of the tangent, the line that just touches the curve at the point. As the second point slides in, the secant swings round into the tangent.

A derivative carries a sign. A positive derivative means the function is rising at that point, and a negative one means it is falling. It is also a different thing from the height. Saying f(4) = 7 and f′(4) = −2 describes a curve at height 7 that is falling by 2 units for each unit moved to the right.

afterFigure.text: Drag the slider to slide the tangent along the curve y = x². On the left of the bottom the tangent tilts down and its slope is negative, and on the right it tilts up. For this curve the slope reported is always twice the x value.

lead.text: Same method, a different point: x = 5. The secant slope has already been simplified for you.

reveal.text: The same move again: let the h term vanish and keep what is left. That limit is the derivative at 5.

lead.text: From x = 3 to x = 4 the secant slope of x² is 7. That averages the whole stretch, so the rate right at 3 can differ.

reveal.text: The rate at x = 3 is 6, below the average of 7 over the next unit, because the curve is still steepening.

blocks.text: A car's odometer reads 40 km at 1:00 and 100 km at 2:30. From those two readings you can say how far the car went and how long it took, and so how fast it went on average. What the readings cannot tell you is how fast the car was going at 2:00 exactly.

That second question is harder than it looks. Speed is distance divided by time, but at a single instant no time passes and no distance is covered. The speed at an instant looks like 0 ÷ 0. The last two lessons showed what to do with 0 ÷ 0: stop standing on the point and look at what happens close to it.

This lesson starts with an average over a stretch and then shrinks the stretch. The average settles on a single number, which is the rate at one instant. The same method gives the steepness of a curve at one point.

blocks.text: Back at the odometer, you turned two readings into an average speed and then replaced the two readings with a shrinking stretch. You found an average rate of 4 for x² between 1 and 3, then watched the slope settle on 2 at x = 1 and on 4 at x = 2.

lessons.title: A rule for powers

lead.text: Every point on a smooth curve has a slope, so the slopes together make a function of their own. Put in x, and out comes the slope of the curve at x. This new function is the derivative of the original, written f′(x).

For y = x² we already know a few of its values. The slope is 2 at x = 1 and 4 at x = 2. It is 6 at x = 3, and the work of the last lesson gave 10 at x = 5. Each of those took a page of algebra, which would be tiresome to repeat for every point.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the same thing from the graph side. The tangent is the straight line that just touches the curve, and its steepness is the slope at that point. Use the buttons to move the point along the curve and read the dot in the lower graph: it sits at the slope you have just seen, 2, 4 or 6. The dots join up into a smooth line, so there is a rule behind the changes. The next question asks you to find it from the numbers above.

lead.text: Look at the slopes listed on the last screen and compare each with its x value.

reveal.text: Each slope is twice its x. That pattern is the derivative of x², f′(x) = 2x.

lead.text: A pattern found from a handful of values needs a reason, so look at where the 2 comes from. The slope of y = x² at x is the limit of the secant slope, and expanding the top and dividing by h leaves 2x + h. As h shrinks the h vanishes and 2x remains.

afterFigure.text: The same sum can be drawn as areas. A square of side x has area x². Make the side x + h and the square gains two strips of area xh and a small corner of area h². The gain is 2xh + h², which is the top of the secant slope, and the corner is the part that vanishes once h shrinks.

Do the same for y = x³. Expanding (x + h)³ gives x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³, so the top of the secant slope is 3x²h + 3xh² + h³. Dividing by h leaves 3x² + 3xh + h². The last two terms vanish as h shrinks, so the slope is 3x².
In general, the expansion of (x + h)ⁿ starts with xⁿ and continues with nxⁿ⁻¹h, and every later term has h² or a higher power in it. Those terms vanish and the term nxⁿ⁻¹ is left.
This is the power rule. In words, bring the power down in front and take one off it. Finding a derivative is called differentiating, so x⁴ differentiates to 4x³ and x⁵ to 5x⁴.

workedSteps.text: Bring the power down and take one off it.
Substitute x = 2.
Calculate.

lead.text: Same two moves: differentiate, then substitute. This time the function is a cube.

reveal.text: You brought the power down, dropped it by one, then substituted. That is the whole power rule.

lead.text: A polynomial is a sum of terms such as 5x², 3x and 7, so we need the derivatives of those parts as well. Three facts cover all of them.

A constant only lifts the whole graph up or down, so every slope stays the same and its derivative is 0. A number multiplying a term stays in front, so the derivative of 5x² is 5 × 2x = 10x. A sum is differentiated one term at a time, and the pieces are added.

afterFigure.text: The picture compares y = x² with y = x² + 3. Slide the tangent along both and you find the same slope at every position, because the second graph is the first lifted up. By the three facts, 3x² + 5x − 4 differentiates to 6x + 5, with the −4 contributing nothing.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate 2x²: keep the 2, bring down the power.
Differentiate 5: a constant.
Add the parts, then substitute x = 1.

lead.text: Apply the power rule to each term and add the results. Constants contribute nothing.

reveal.text: Each term gave its own piece: 6x from the square and −2 from the line, while the constant added nothing.

lead.text: Once f′(x) is a formula, it answers two kinds of question. Put in an x and it gives the slope there. Set it equal to a number and solve, and it tells you where the curve has that slope.

Take f(x) = x² + 4x, which differentiates to f′(x) = 2x + 4. The slope is 4 at x = 0, so the curve is rising there, and −2 at x = −3, so it is falling. At x = −2 the slope is 0 and the tangent is flat. Solving 2x + 4 = 0 finds that point directly.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the two pictures and slide the tangent. It tilts down on the left of x = −2, lies flat at x = −2 and tilts up to the right. A negative slope describes the direction the curve is travelling, and the height itself can still be positive.

lead.text: The height 4 − x² peaks at x = 0. On the left it rises, and on the right it falls.

reveal.text: f′(x) = −2x, so the slope at 1 is negative and the curve is falling. A negative rate does not make the height negative.

blocks.text: In the last lesson we found that the curve y = x² has slope 2 at x = 1 and slope 4 at x = 2. Each answer took a line of algebra with a shrinking h, and every new point needed a fresh calculation.

Doing that for a hundred points would take all day, and a curve like y = x⁵ would be worse. But the answers 2 and 4 hint at something. If the slopes follow a pattern, one formula could hand us the slope anywhere.

This lesson finds that formula for powers of x and explains why it works. It then extends it to whole polynomials by handling one term at a time, and uses the formula to say where a curve rises, falls or lies flat.

intro.promise: By the end you'll differentiate any polynomial term by term, and read the sign of the result.

recap.keyIdea: Bring the power down and take one off it, term by term; constants vanish and multiples stay.

blocks.text: Back at the table of slopes, you found the pattern for x² and saw the algebra behind it. You differentiated x⁴ to 4x³ and found a slope of 32 at 2, and you found that 4 − x² has slope −2 at 1.

lessons.title: A function inside a function

lead.text: Suppose you are paid £15 an hour, and each pound buys 1.2 euros. Your pay is a rate of 15 pounds per hour, and the exchange is a rate of 1.2 euros per pound. Together, 15 × 1.2 = 18 euros arrive for each hour you work.

The hours came first and the euros last, with pounds as the stage in between. To get the rate from hours to euros we multiplied the rates of the two stages. The units show why: euros per pound times pounds per hour leaves euros per hour, because the pounds cancel.
This holds for any chain of stages, and it is what the pedals and the wheel do on a bicycle. The distance covered per second is the product of the rate at each stage.

lead.text: Now the bicycle itself.

reveal.text: You multiplied the three rates: 1 × 3 × 2 = 6 metres each second. Each stage multiplies what the one before it produced.

lead.text: The same structure appears in a formula. In f(x) = (4x + 5)² there are two stages. The inner function u = 4x + 5 turns x into a number, and the outer function u² squares that number. Move x up by 1 and u moves up by 4, so the inner stage has rate 4.

The outer stage squares u, and by the power rule its rate is 2u. That rate depends on the current value of u, so it has to be measured at the value the inner stage has produced. Multiplying the two rates gives the rate of the whole formula.
This is the chain rule: the outer rate, taken at the inner value, times the inner rate.

afterFigure.text: Compare the two graphs by sliding the tangent along each. The slope of (4x + 5)² is four times the slope of (x + 5)² at the same x, because the inner stage of the first runs four times as fast as x and the inner stage of the second keeps pace with it.

workedSteps.text: Name the inner function. At x = 1 it equals 1.
The outer function, u², changes at rate 2u.
The inner function changes at 4 per unit of x.
Multiply the two rates.

lead.text: Same moves: name the inner function, find both rates, multiply. This time the inside is 2x + 1.

reveal.text: You took the outer rate at the inner value, then multiplied by how fast the inside moves. Without the second factor the answer would be too small.

lead.text: The inner rate can be negative. Take f(x) = (4 − x)². The inner function u = 4 − x goes down by 1 when x goes up by 1, so its rate is −1. The outer rate is still 2u, and the product is 2(4 − x) × (−1) = −2(4 − x).

The minus sign has a meaning. For x below 4 the bracket is positive, so the derivative is negative and the curve falls as x rises. At x = 4 the bracket is zero, so the slope is zero and the graph is flat at the bottom of its dip. Beyond 4 the derivative turns positive.

afterFigure.text: The pictures show (4 − x)² before and after its lowest point. Slide the tangent and watch it tilt down on the left and up on the right.

workedSteps.text: Inner function and its rate.
Outer rate.
Multiply by the inner rate, then put in x = 1.

lead.text: Say the rates out loud: the outer rate at the inside, then the inner rate.

reveal.text: The 6 is 2 × 3: the outer rate's 2 times the inner rate of 3, kept beside the inner expression 3x + 1.

lead.text: Chains of rates are not limited to formulas written in x. Suppose a square patch of mould has a side of s centimetres, and the side grows at 2 centimetres a day. The area is A = s², which by the power rule changes at 2s square centimetres for each centimetre of side.

When the side is 10 cm, the area changes at 2 × 10 = 20 square centimetres per centimetre of side, and the side grows at 2 centimetres per day. So the area grows at 20 × 2 = 40 square centimetres per day, and the two rates have multiplied just as they did for the pedals and the wheel.
The pattern needs only that one quantity depends on a second, and the second on a third. The rate of the first with respect to the third is then the product of the two stage rates.

blocks.text: A bicycle passes your effort along in stages. The pedals turn, the chain makes the back wheel turn faster than the pedals, and the wheel rolls the bike forward. Change any one stage and the speed changes.

To find the bike's speed you do not need to know how each stage works inside. You need the rate of each: how many wheel turns come from one pedal turn, and how many metres one wheel turn covers. The speed is those rates combined.

The same structure turns up in formulas. When one expression sits inside another, as in (4x + 5)², the power rule alone gives the wrong slope. This lesson shows how to combine the rates of the two stages, and uses the bicycle to explain why.

recap.keyIdea: Rates in a chain multiply: differentiate the outer function at the inner value, then multiply by the inner function's rate.

blocks.text: Back on the bicycle, you found that it covers 6 metres each second by multiplying 1 × 3 × 2. You used the same multiplication to get 8 for (4x − 3)² at x = 1, and you saw a falling inside turn the slope negative.

recap.nextHook: Derivatives measure rates, and the commonest rate is speed. The next lesson follows a moving object through its position, velocity and acceleration.

lessons.title: Read motion from a curve

lead.text: Start with something simpler than a lift: a walk along a straight path. At 10 seconds you are 20 metres from the gate, and at 20 seconds you are 35 metres from it. In those 10 seconds your position changed by 15 metres, so you covered 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 metres every second.

That number is the rate of change of your position. When we also keep track of which way you are going, it is called velocity, and it is measured in metres per second, written m/s. If you keep the same pace, the velocity is the same at every moment, and a graph of position against time is a straight line. The velocity is the slope of that line.

Real motion is rarely so tidy. A lift gains and loses pace along the way, so its position graph bends. Dividing the change in position by the change in time then gives only an average over the stretch, and the next screen turns to the velocity at a single moment.
Use the walk's arithmetic on a lift. It rises at a steady pace, and it is 10 m above the ground at 2 seconds and 16 m above it at 5 seconds.

reveal.text: You divided the 6 m gained by the 3 seconds it took. For a steady pace that is the slope of the straight position graph.

lead.text: Now let a car pull away from traffic lights, with its distance from the lights after t seconds given by s(t) = 4t² metres. The graph of s against t curves upwards, because the car covers more ground in each second than in the one before.

A steady rate is the slope of a straight position graph. Here the graph bends, so to ask how fast the car is going at one moment we use the slope of the tangent at that moment. That slope is the derivative, so the velocity at time t is v(t) = s′(t). For s(t) = 4t² the power rule gives v(t) = 8t.

afterFigure.text: Put in some times. At t = 1 the tangent has slope 8, so the car is moving at 8 m/s, and at t = 3 the slope is 24 and it has reached 24 m/s. Switch between the two pictures to watch the tangent steepen as the car gains pace. The steady walk is the case where the tangent and the graph are the same line.

lead.text: Same first move as the car: take one derivative of position, then put in the time.

reveal.text: You differentiated position, then substituted the time. The slope of the position graph at that instant is the velocity, not the distance travelled.

lead.text: Look again at the car. At 1 second it moves at 8 m/s and at 3 seconds at 24 m/s, so its velocity is changing too. Any quantity that changes has a rate, and the rate at which velocity changes is called acceleration.

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, which makes it the derivative of the derivative of position. That is the second derivative, written s″(t). For the car v(t) = 8t, so the acceleration is 8. The unit tells the same story. Velocity is in metres per second, and each second adds another 8 metres per second, so acceleration is in metres per second per second, written m/s².

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the car's velocity v(t) = 8t as a graph of its own. It is a straight line that climbs 8 m/s for every second, and its slope is the acceleration. The tangent has the same slope at 1 second and at 3 seconds, which is what a steady acceleration looks like.

steps.headline: For s(t) = 3t² − t metres, find the velocity and the acceleration at t = 2 seconds.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate once to get velocity.
Put in t = 2.
Differentiate again to get acceleration.

steps.headline: For s(t) = t³ metres, find the acceleration at t = 1 second.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate once to get velocity.
Differentiate again, then put in t = 1.

lead.text: Every velocity so far has been positive, but a position can also fall. Take a toy car on a straight track with s(t) = t² − 8t metres, measured from a mark on the track. Its velocity is v(t) = 2t − 8, which at t = 1 is −6 m/s.

The minus sign carries the direction. A positive velocity means the car is moving the way position is counted, away from the mark, and a negative velocity means it is moving back towards it. At t = 4 the velocity is zero and the car pauses to turn round. At t = 5 it is +2 m/s and the car is heading away from the mark again.

afterFigure.text: Sometimes only the size of the velocity matters, and that size is called the speed. A car at −6 m/s and a car at +6 m/s have opposite velocities and the same speed, 6 m/s. Speed cannot be negative. In the pictures the position graph falls while the car rolls back and rises once it has turned.

lead.text: Read the sign of the slope on the position graph. A falling graph is motion in the negative direction.

reveal.text: The slope was negative, so the velocity was negative. The object was moving backwards.

lead.text: One more difference needs care. Dividing a change in position by the change in time gives the average velocity over a stretch, and the velocity at one moment can be quite different from it.

Take s(t) = 2t² metres between 1 s and 3 s. The position goes from 2 m to 18 m, a gain of 16 m in 2 s, so the average velocity is 8 m/s. The object keeps speeding up through that stretch, though. Its velocity v(t) = 4t is 4 m/s at the start and 12 m/s at the end, and the average sits somewhere between.

afterFigure.text: The picture draws both lines on the same curve. The line across the whole stretch is the average, and its slope is 8. The tangent at 3 seconds is steeper, because the object is moving faster at the end of the stretch than it was on average.

lead.text: A stone's position is s(t) = t² metres. Between 1 s and 3 s it covers 8 m, an average velocity of 4 m/s. The question is about the end of that stretch alone.

reveal.text: You differentiated and put in 3. The stone is still speeding up, so its velocity at the end of the stretch is greater than the average over it.

lessons.orientation: Differentiate position for velocity and velocity for acceleration, with units.

blocks.text: Step into a lift in a tall building and press the button for the top floor. The doors close, and for a moment nothing seems to happen. Then you feel a gentle push into the floor, and the number on the display starts to climb. After a few seconds the push fades and the lift glides up at an even pace. Near the top you feel a little light as it slows, and then it stops.

Your height changed the whole way up, but the ride felt different from one moment to the next. At the start the lift was gaining pace, and near the end it was losing it, with an even stretch in between. Each of those is a fact about a rate. The last lesson showed that a derivative measures a rate of change, and a lift is the most familiar place to meet one.

This lesson follows one moving object. It starts from the object's position on a graph and works out how fast the object is going. After that it asks how quickly that rate is changing, and which way the object is heading.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read how fast and which way something moves from its position formula, and how quickly that is changing.
intro.whyItMatters: Every moving thing, from a ball to a train, is described by position, velocity and acceleration.

recap.keyIdea: Differentiate position for velocity, and again for acceleration. Velocity has a sign; speed is its size.

blocks.text: You began with a lift that rose 6 m in 3 seconds, a steady 2 m/s. For 3t² − t you found a velocity of 11 m/s at 2 s and an acceleration of 6 m/s². A velocity of −6 m/s showed a toy car rolling backwards. For s(t) = t², the velocity at 3 s was 6 m/s, above the average of 4 m/s over the stretch before it.

recap.nextHook: When the velocity falls to zero, an object stops for an instant before it turns round. The next lesson uses that idea to find where a curve turns.

lessons.title: Where does the curve turn?

steps.headline: The slope at the top of a throw

lead.text: A ball thrown straight up shows what a slope does at a turning point. On the way up its height is increasing, so the slope of its height graph is positive. On the way down the height is decreasing, so the slope is negative.

Between those two stretches there is an instant when the ball has stopped climbing and has not yet started to fall. The slope cannot jump from positive to negative without passing through zero, so at that instant it is exactly zero and the tangent to the graph is flat. A point where the slope is zero is called a stationary point.

afterFigure.text: In the pictures the curve is 4x − x². The tangent tilts up while the curve climbs, lies flat at the top and tilts down once the curve is falling. Switch between the pictures to watch the tilt change sign. The next screen gives a ball's heights as numbers and asks you to find the top from them.

lead.text: A ball is thrown straight up. Its heights in metres at 0, 1, 2 and so on up to 7 seconds are 0, 9, 16, 21, 24, 25, 24, 21.

reveal.text: The gains shrank from 9 m to 1 m and then became losses. The slope changed sign there, so the top is where it passed through zero.

lead.text: A table of heights finds the top of a throw only to the nearest second, and a formula can find it exactly. The ball in the table follows h(t) = 10t − t² metres. Its slope is h′(t) = 10 − 2t, and the top of the throw is where that slope is zero.

So the method is to differentiate, set the derivative equal to zero and solve. Here 10 − 2t = 0 gives t = 5, the second you read from the table. Putting t = 5 back into the original formula gives the height there, 10 × 5 − 5² = 25 m, the largest value in the list. The solution says where the turning point is, and the original formula says how high it is.

A turning point like this one is a local maximum, a point higher than everything near it on the curve. The word local matters because a curve can have several peaks, and each is only the highest in its own neighbourhood.

steps.headline: Find the local maximum of f(x) = 12x − x².

lead.text: Here is the whole method on one formula, from the slope to the height of the peak.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate.
Set the slope to zero and solve.
Check either side: the slope is positive before 6 and negative after.
Find the height at x = 6.

lead.text: Same first two moves as the worked example: differentiate, then set the slope to zero.

reveal.text: You set the slope to zero and solved. That gives the x value of the candidate turning point.

lead.text: Setting the slope to zero finds candidates, and each one needs a closer look. Take f(x) = x² − 2x, whose slope is 2x − 2. The slope is zero at x = 1. A step to the left, at x = 0, the slope is −2 and the curve is falling. A step to the right, at x = 2, it is +2 and the curve is rising.

Falling and then rising makes a dip, which is called a local minimum. Rising and then falling makes a peak, the local maximum from before. The sign of the slope on either side of the stationary point tells you which one you have.

afterFigure.text: There is a third possibility. If the slope is zero at a point but has the same sign on both sides, the curve flattens for a moment and carries on in the same direction. That is no turn at all, so a zero slope on its own is not enough to say that there is one. Switch between the pictures to see the sign change at this dip.

lead.text: Use the power rule to find the slope a little to the left of 0 and a little to the right of it.

reveal.text: The slope was positive on both sides of 0, so the curve kept rising through the flat point. A zero slope alone did not make a turn.

lead.text: Often a question concerns only part of a curve, such as the first six seconds of a throw. A stretch that includes both of its end points is called a closed interval, and [a, b] is the short way of writing one.

On a closed interval the highest value is not always at a turning point. Take f(x) = x² − 4x on [0, 5]. Its slope 2x − 4 is zero at x = 2, and f(2) = −4 is the lowest value on the stretch. After x = 2 the curve climbs to the edge, where f(5) = 5. The highest value is at an end.

So the method has one more step. Find the stationary points inside the interval, work out the function at each of them and at both ends, and compare the numbers. The largest is the highest value on the interval and the smallest is the lowest.
Check for a stationary point first. If the slope is never zero, only the two ends are left to compare.

reveal.text: The slope of 2x + 1 is 2 everywhere, so there is no turning point. The line keeps rising, and its highest value is at the right end.

lead.text: The graph of x² has one stationary point, at 0. The interval is [−1, 2]. Compare the ends with it.

reveal.text: You compared the ends with the stationary point at 0. The stationary point is the lowest value here, and the highest is at an end, which a search for zero slope alone would miss.

lessons.orientation: Use slope signs to identify local extrema and check endpoints for an absolute maximum.

blocks.text: Throw a ball straight up and watch it. It leaves your hand fast and slows as it climbs. For an instant at the top it seems to hang there, and then it drops back, faster and faster.

That instant matters in a great many questions. The top of a throw and the bottom of a valley are both places where something stops rising and starts falling, or stops falling and starts rising. Finding those places by eye works for a ball, but it is not much use when all you have is a formula.

This lesson uses the slope to find those turning places exactly. It starts from what the slope does as the ball goes up and over, and it ends with two warnings: a flat spot can fool you into seeing a turn that is not there, and the highest value on a stretch can sit at its edge.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find and check the turning points of a curve, and find its highest value on an interval.
intro.whyItMatters: Finding the best value, the highest or the lowest, is what turning points are for.

recap.keyIdea: A curve can turn only where its slope is zero. Check the slope either side, and on an interval compare the ends too.

blocks.text: Back with the thrown ball, the formula put the top at 5 seconds, where the table had shown it. You found the peak of 12x − x² at x = 6, with height 36. You also saw that x³ is flat at 0 without turning, and that the highest value of x² on [−1, 2] sits at an end.

recap.nextHook: Everything so far has gone from a formula to its rate. The next lesson goes the other way and asks what formula a given rate came from.

lessons.title: Undo a rate of change

steps.headline: From a rate back to a position

lead.text: Picture a cyclist riding along a straight road at a steady 5 metres per second. When we start the clock she is 20 metres past a signpost. After 6 seconds she has ridden 5 × 6 = 30 metres, so she is 20 + 30 = 50 metres past the signpost.

As a formula, her position after t seconds is s(t) = 20 + 5t. Differentiate it and you get 5, the rate we began with, because the 20 is a constant and a constant has slope zero. We reached the formula by asking which formula has 5 as its rate, and then adding the place where she started.

That is the shape of the whole lesson. Given a rate, we look for a formula whose derivative is that rate, and we use a known starting value to finish the job. The next screens meet rates that change, where the search for the formula needs more care, but the starting value will do the same work.
Now a car. It moves at a steady 4 m/s and starts 10 m from the start line.

reveal.text: The car covers 12 m in 3 seconds and began 10 m out. The distance travelled plus the starting point gives the position.

lead.text: Now a rate that changes. Suppose a runner's velocity at time x is 6x. We want a position formula F(x) whose derivative is 6x. The power rule suggests F(x) = 3x², because 3x² differentiates to 3 × 2x = 6x. A function found this way, whose derivative is the rate we started with, is called an antiderivative of that rate.

There is a catch, and the cyclist has already shown it. Differentiating 3x² + 4 also gives 6x, and so does 3x² − 9, because a constant disappears when you differentiate. Every vertical shift of the graph has the same slope at every x. So 6x has no single antiderivative. It has a whole family of them, 3x² + C, where C stands for any constant.

afterFigure.text: The two curves in the pictures have the same shape, with one raised above the other. At any given x their slopes match. Which member of the family is the right one depends on information that the rate cannot supply, such as where the runner started. For the cyclist it was the 20 metres.

lead.text: Think about what raising or lowering a whole graph does to its slope.

reveal.text: Shifting x² up or down leaves every slope alone, so every shift is an antiderivative of 2x. The family is x² + C.

lead.text: A known value picks one member of the family. Take the rate 6x again, which gives F(x) = 3x² + C. Suppose we are told that F(1) = 5. Putting x = 1 into the family gives 3 + C = 5, which means C = 2. The one function that fits is F(x) = 3x² + 2.

This follows the cyclist's pattern. The rate gives the shape of the answer, and one known value fixes where that shape sits. For the cyclist the known value was the 20 metres at time zero. Time zero is the commonest choice, because putting x = 0 into a formula often removes every term except the constant.
You can always check an antiderivative by differentiating it. If the result is the rate you were given, the formula is right. The constant never affects this check.
Same move as the example: put the known input into the family and solve for C.

reveal.text: You put the known value into the family and solved for C. That one number picks a single graph out of all the shifted copies.

lead.text: For a rate like 6x we could guess the antiderivative. For 12x² or 5x⁴ we want a method that always works, and it comes from the power rule. Differentiating xⁿ brings the power down in front and takes one off the power. To undo that, make the two moves in the opposite order: add one to the power, then divide by the new power.

So the antiderivative of x² is x³ ÷ 3, and the antiderivative of 5x⁴ is 5x⁵ ÷ 5 = x⁵. In symbols, the whole family of antiderivatives is written with an integral sign and is called the indefinite integral of the rate.

The rule works for every power except −1, which this course does not need. A rate with several terms is undone one term at a time, and a plain number such as 2 undoes to 2x because 2x has slope 2. Differentiate the result to check it.

workedSteps.text: Undo the rate: add one to the power, divide by it.
Use F(0) = 1 to fix C.
Put in x = 1.
Undo the rate.
Use F(0) = 0 to fix C.
Put in x = 2.

lead.text: The rate has two terms this time. Undo each, fix the constant, then evaluate. You can check by differentiating your answer.

reveal.text: Differentiating x³ + 2x + 1 gives back 3x² + 2, so the answer checks. Undoing a derivative can always be tested by differentiating.

lessons.orientation: Recover a family of antiderivatives and use an initial value to fix the constant.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A car sets off from a point somewhere past the start line, and its speedometer holds steady. You cannot see the car. You have the speedometer reading and a note of where the car began. The puzzle is to say where the car is after a few seconds.

Everything so far in the course has gone one way, from where something is to how fast it is changing. This puzzle goes the other way. The rate is known, and the position is what we want. Working backwards from a rate to the thing it came from is the subject of this lesson.

There turns out to be a catch. A rate on its own does not say where the car began, so the answer comes with an unknown that only a starting position can fix. The lesson shows what that unknown is and how to find it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll recover a function from its rate and use a known value to pin down the constant.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing how fast something changes and where it started tells you where it is.

recap.keyIdea: Undoing a derivative gives a family F(x) + C; one known value fixes C and picks out the function.

blocks.text: You began with a cyclist at 5 m/s and a car that ends up 22 m from the line. You then undid 12x² to get 4x³ + C, and used F(0) = 1 to find F(1) = 5. For F′(x) = 3x² + 2 with F(0) = 1, you found F(2) = 13.

recap.nextHook: Undoing a rate gave a position from a known start. The next lesson reaches the same kind of answer another way, by cutting the area under a rate graph into thin strips.

lessons.title: Build an area from strips

steps.headline: Rate times time makes an amount

lead.text: Start with the easiest tap. It runs at 3 litres per minute for 4 minutes, so it delivers 3 × 4 = 12 litres. Draw this as a graph with time along the bottom and the flow rate up the side, and it is a rectangle 4 minutes wide and 3 litres per minute tall.

The area of that rectangle is its width times its height, which is 4 × 3 = 12. The units multiply as well, since minutes times litres per minute leaves litres. So the area under a rate graph is an amount of water. A tap that changes in steps is handled by adding one rectangle for each stretch where the rate holds still.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the same tap running for 4 minutes and for 2 minutes. The shorter run gives a rectangle half as wide, and the amount halves with it. Real taps are seldom so tidy, and the rest of the lesson shows how thin rectangles cope when the flow keeps changing.

lead.text: A tank fills at 2 litres per minute for 3 minutes. Then the rate rises to 4 litres per minute for 2 minutes.

reveal.text: You drew two rectangles, 3 minutes by 2 litres per minute and 2 minutes by 4. Their areas are amounts of water, and the amounts add.

lead.text: Now suppose the tap is turned up smoothly, so that t minutes after you start the flow is 2t litres per minute. At the start nothing is flowing, and after 3 minutes the rate has reached 6 litres per minute. The graph of the rate is a sloping line, and no single rectangle fits under it.

So cut the 3 minutes into strips of one minute each and pretend the rate stays fixed during every strip. For each strip take the rate at its left edge, which is the value at the start of that minute. The rates at 0, 1 and 2 minutes are 0, 2 and 4 litres per minute, and the three rectangles have areas 1 × 0, 1 × 2 and 1 × 4. Together they add up to 6 litres.

afterFigure.text: Adding up rectangles like this gives a rectangle sum. A strip whose height is read at its left edge is a left-endpoint rectangle. The picture shows the three rectangles and then six thinner ones. Each rectangle sits under the line, so the sum falls short of the true amount. The next screens show by how much.

steps.headline: Use three left-endpoint rectangles for f(x) = x on [0, 3].

workedSteps.text: Width: the interval length over the number of strips.
Left edges are 0, 1 and 2, so the heights are 0, 1 and 2.
Add width × height for each strip.

lead.text: Split [0, 4] into two equal strips. Take each height at the left edge, then add width × height.

reveal.text: You took the height at each left edge and added the two strips. That is a left-endpoint sum.

steps.headline: The other edge of the strip

lead.text: Reading the rate at the left edge of each strip was a choice. We could equally read it at the right edge, the value at the end of each minute. For the same tap the rates at 1, 2 and 3 minutes are 2, 4 and 6 litres per minute, and the three right-endpoint rectangles add up to 1 × (2 + 4 + 6) = 12 litres.

Now compare the two estimates with the exact amount, 9 litres, which is the area of the triangle under the line: half of 3 minutes times 6 litres per minute. The left estimate of 6 is too small and the right estimate of 12 is too large. That is no accident. This rate only rises, so within every strip the left edge is the lowest value and the right edge is the highest.

afterFigure.text: As the pictures show, the left rectangles sit under the graph and the right rectangles poke out above it. The exact amount must lie between the two sums, and the gap between them tells you how good the estimate is. That gap is 12 − 6 = 6 litres for these strips, and thinner strips will shrink it.

steps.headline: Use four right-endpoint rectangles for f(x) = x on [0, 4].

workedSteps.text: Width: 4 over 4 strips.
Right edges are 1, 2, 3 and 4, so those are the heights.
Add width × height for each strip.

lead.text: Halve the width of the strips and the two estimates close in. With six strips of half a minute each, the left rectangles have heights 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, and the sum is 0.5 × 15 = 7.5 litres. The right rectangles have heights 1 to 6 and give 0.5 × 21 = 10.5 litres. The gap has shrunk from 6 litres to 3, and the exact 9 still lies between them.

Keep halving and the gap keeps shrinking, because the left and right heights of each strip differ by less and less. The number that both sums approach as the strips become thinner is the exact amount. It is called the definite integral of the rate over the interval, and for a straight-line rate it equals the area of the neat shape under it, like the 9-litre triangle.

afterFigure.text: A third choice of height often lands closer: the value halfway across the strip, which gives a midpoint rectangle. On a straight line the rectangle sticks out above the line on one side of the strip's centre and leaves a gap below it on the other, and the two small triangles are the same size. A midpoint sum is exact there, as the third picture shows with the 9 litres.

lead.text: Think about where the left edge of a strip sits compared with the rest of the strip.

reveal.text: On a rising graph the left edge is the lowest point of its strip, so every left rectangle sits under the graph and the left sum cannot be too large.

lead.text: A midpoint rectangle takes its height at the strip's centre. Try it on the line f(x) = x over [0, 4] with two strips.

reveal.text: Centre heights 1 and 3, times width 2, gave the exact area under the line. For a straight line the midpoint sum has no error.

lessons.orientation: Approximate an integral with equal-width rectangles and compare sampling choices.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Fill a bath and you can see how much water has gone in by looking at the level. Now suppose you cannot see the bath. All you have is a dial on the tap that says how many litres per minute are flowing. You leave the tap running while you do something else, nudging it now and then, and later you want to know how much water is in the bath.

Working that out from the dial alone is a different job from anything so far. Earlier lessons went from an amount to its rate by taking derivatives, and the last one went from a rate back to an amount by undoing them. This lesson finds an amount from a rate by a third route, one that needs only multiplication and addition.

The route is to draw the rate against time and measure the area underneath it with thin rectangles. We start with a tap that changes in steps and end with a rate that changes smoothly, where thinner rectangles give a sharper answer.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate an accumulated total with rectangle sums, and say how the estimate closes in on the exact amount.
intro.whyItMatters: Any amount built from a changing rate, such as water, distance or cost, is an area under a graph.

recap.keyIdea: Add width × height strip by strip. Thinner strips squeeze the sum towards the definite integral.

blocks.text: You began with a tank filling at 2 litres per minute and then 4, which took in 14 litres. For a rising tap, left strips gave 6 litres and right strips 12, with the exact 9 between them. For f(x) = x over [0, 4], two left strips gave 4 and four right strips gave 10. Two midpoint strips gave the exact 8.

recap.nextHook: So far every rate has been positive. The next lesson looks at a bath that drains as well as fills, where some of the area under the graph counts against the total.

lessons.title: When areas cancel

lead.text: Take a sink that you fill and then let drain. The tap runs at 5 litres per minute for 2 minutes, which adds 5 × 2 = 10 litres. Then you pull the plug and it drains at 3 litres per minute for 4 minutes, which takes away 3 × 4 = 12 litres. The change in the water is 10 − 12 = −2 litres, so the sink ends with 2 litres less than it began with. That total, once gains and losses are put together, is the net change.

To show this on a rate graph the rates need signs. A rate of +5 litres per minute means water coming in, and a rate of −3 means water going out. The draining stretch then lies below the time axis, as a rectangle 4 minutes wide and −3 tall. Its area is 4 × (−3) = −12. The minus sign says that the water left.

afterFigure.text: So the net change is still a sum of rectangle areas, but a rectangle under the axis counts as negative. In the pictures the filling rectangle sits above the axis and the draining one below it. That one rule is what the rest of the lesson builds on.

lead.text: A bath fills at 3 litres per minute for 4 minutes. Then the plug is pulled, and it drains at 2 litres per minute for 3 minutes.

reveal.text: Filling added water and draining took it away. Putting the two stretches together, with the draining counted as negative, gives the net change.

lead.text: Now let the rate change smoothly across zero. Take the line f(x) = x between x = −1 and x = 2. Below zero the line sits under the axis, where the rate is negative. Above zero it sits over the axis. The shape is two triangles that meet at the origin.

The triangle on the left has base 1 and height 1, so its size is ½ × 1 × 1 = 0.5. It lies below the axis, so it counts as −0.5. The triangle on the right has base 2 and height 2, so it counts as +2. Adding the signed pieces gives −0.5 + 2 = 1.5. This total is called the signed area, and it is the value of the definite integral. In the sink's terms it is the net change, the gain minus the loss.

afterFigure.text: The pictures show the whole stretch and then only its left triangle. The part below the axis takes away from the total and the part above adds to it. A graph that crosses the axis is split where it crosses, and each piece is treated on its own.

lead.text: A constant rate below the axis is one rectangle with a negative height.

reveal.text: The rate was negative, so the region counted as negative. The size of the region is 6, and the signed area is −6.

steps.headline: Find the signed area of f(x) = x from −3 to 1.

lead.text: Here is the same split-and-add method on a line that crosses the axis.

workedSteps.text: The graph crosses the axis at x = 0, so split there.
Left triangle: base 3, height 3, below the axis.
Right triangle: base 1, height 1, above the axis.
Add the signed pieces.

steps.headline: Find the signed area of f(x) = x from −2 to 2.

workedSteps.text: Left triangle: base 2, height 2, below the axis.
Right triangle: base 2, height 2, above the axis.
Add the signed pieces.

lead.text: Signed area answers the question of how much the amount changed. Sometimes the question is simply how much ground a region covers. Think of painting the region between a graph and the axis, where it takes the same paint above the axis as below. For that you want the total area, which counts every piece as positive.

Go back to f(x) = x between −1 and 2. The two pieces have sizes 0.5 and 2, so the total area is 0.5 + 2 = 2.5, while the signed area was 1.5. Total area adds the sizes and ignores the signs. Signed area keeps the signs, so pieces can cancel each other.

When two pieces have the same size and opposite signs, the signed area is exactly zero even though a lot of area is there. A signed area of zero says that the gains and losses balance. It does not say that the graph is flat or that nothing happened.
You have already found the signed area of this graph. Now ask a different question of it.

reveal.text: Each triangle has size 2, so the total area is 2 + 2 = 4, even though the signed area of the same graph is 0.

lead.text: So far we have always travelled from a smaller x to a larger one. The two x values that mark the ends of a stretch are called its bounds, and they can be given in either order. If the definite integral of a rate from 0 to 4 is 10 litres, the integral from 4 back to 0 is −10 litres.

The bath explains the sign. Running the clock forwards from 0 to 4 minutes adds 10 litres. Running it backwards from 4 to 0 undoes that and takes the 10 litres out again. The graph is the same graph and the area has the same size. Only the direction of travel has changed, and travelling the other way reverses the sign.
So swapping the bounds changes the sign of the integral and nothing else. The next lesson makes use of this when it joins integrals to derivatives.
The same curve, travelled the other way: from 3 back to 1.

reveal.text: Running the stretch backwards flipped the sign and left the size unchanged.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish signed accumulation from geometric area and reverse integral bounds correctly.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Think of a bath that you fill and then let drain. While the tap runs, the water level climbs. When you pull the plug, it falls. At every moment water is flowing in or out. The level at the end depends on how much came in and how much went out.

The last lesson measured an amount as the area under a rate graph. That worked because every rate was positive, so every rectangle added water. A rate that takes water away has to count against the total, and the graph needs a way to show it.

This lesson gives that way, using negative rates. It then asks what it means for areas to cancel, how that differs from the ordinary size of an area, and what happens when you read a graph from right to left.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the signed area under a graph and explain how it differs from total area.
intro.whyItMatters: Net change, such as profit or displacement, is a signed integral.

recap.keyIdea: A definite integral counts regions above the axis as positive and below as negative. Total area adds the sizes.

blocks.text: You found that a sink ends 2 litres down after filling and draining, and that the bath nets 6 litres. The signed area of x from −3 to 1 came to −4, and x on [−2, 2] cancelled to 0 although its total area is 4. Reversing the bounds of an integral of 6 gave −6.

recap.nextHook: Areas under a rate and undone derivatives have now both given amounts from rates. The next lesson shows that they are one idea, and that it turns every area problem into a subtraction.

lessons.title: Rates and areas connect

lead.text: Start with the bath from the opener. After t minutes the tap delivers 2t litres per minute, so at 1 minute it delivers 2 litres per minute and at 2 minutes it delivers 4. Draw that rate against time and you get a straight line rising from the origin. The area under the line is the water that has flowed in.

Take the first two minutes. The area under the line is a triangle with a base of 2 minutes and a height of 4 litres per minute, so it is ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 litres. The units agree with this: minutes multiplied by litres per minute leave litres.

afterFigure.text: The first minute alone gives a triangle with a base of 1 and a height of 2, so its area is ½ × 1 × 2 = 1 litre. Triangles work here because the rate is a straight line from zero. Most rates have no such tidy shape, and a method that only handles neat shapes will not carry us far. The next screens look for one that does.

lead.text: Use the same triangle method on the first three minutes of the tap.

reveal.text: You found 9 litres from a triangle. That is more than the 4 litres of the first two minutes, because the tap keeps opening. The next screen reaches this 9 a second way.

lead.text: Now count the same water another way. Instead of finding one area at a time, keep a running total. Let A(x) be the litres that have run in by minute x. The triangles give A(1) = 1 and A(2) = 4, and the last screen gave A(3) = 9.
Each total is the square of its minute. The triangle up to minute x has a base of x and a height of 2x, so its area is ½ × x × 2x = x². The running total is A(x) = x².

afterFigure.text: Compare that with the lesson on undoing derivatives. The derivative of x² is 2x, which is the tap's rate, so x² is an antiderivative of 2x. This is no coincidence. The rate says how fast the water is arriving at each moment, so the slope of the running total has to equal the rate. A curve whose slope is 2x at every point is an antiderivative of 2x.

cases.label: Slope of the total at minute 2

steps.headline: Subtracting the totals at the two ends

lead.text: The running total gives a quick way to find the water that arrives in the middle of a run. Suppose you want the water that flows in between minute 2 and minute 3. By minute 3 the total is A(3) = 9 litres, and 4 of those had already arrived by minute 2. What is left is 9 − 4 = 5 litres.

The picture confirms it. Between minutes 2 and 3 the region under the line is a strip 1 minute wide, with heights 4 and 6 at its sides. Its area is the average height, 5, times the width, 1, which is 5 litres. The subtraction and the geometry agree.

afterFigure.text: In general, the area under a rate from a to b is the running total at b minus the running total at a, and the running total is an antiderivative F of the rate.
This is the fundamental theorem of calculus. To find an area under a rate you find an antiderivative, put in the two ends and subtract. No rectangles or triangles are needed.

steps.headline: Find the integral of 4x + 3 from 1 to 2.

lead.text: Here is the whole method on a rate with two terms.

workedSteps.text: Undo the rate one term at a time.
Put in the top end and the bottom end.
Subtract, top minus bottom.

steps.headline: Find the integral of 2x + 1 from 0 to 2.

workedSteps.text: Undo each term of the rate.
Put in the ends and subtract.

lead.text: One loose end remains. Earlier in the course a rate turned out to have a whole family of antiderivatives, F(x) + C, one for every constant C. That leaves a choice about which of them goes into the subtraction.

Take F(x) = x² and G(x) = x² + 4, and use both on the tap's rate between minute 1 and minute 3. With F the total is 9 − 1 = 8 litres. With G it is (9 + 4) − (1 + 4) = 13 − 5 = 8 litres. The 4 is added at the top end and taken away again at the bottom end, so it leaves no trace.

The same happens for any constant. Using F + C gives (F(b) + C) − (F(a) + C), and the two Cs cancel to leave F(b) − F(a). That is why a definite integral is a single number even though its antiderivative is a whole family, and why you may take C = 0 and leave the constant out.
Think about what happens to a constant that is added to F when you put in the top end and then the bottom end.

reveal.text: The same constant was added to F(b) and to F(a), so subtracting one from the other removed it.

steps.headline: How fast the running total grows

lead.text: Back to the running total, now for any rate f. Let A(x) be the amount that has built up from a fixed starting time up to x. It is the area under f between the start and x, and it is called an accumulation function.

As x increases, the right-hand end of the area moves. Push it a tiny step to the right and the area gains a thin sliver. The sliver is almost a rectangle as wide as the step and as tall as the rate at that moment, f(x). So the gain per unit of step is f(x), which says that the accumulation grows at the rate f(x) at its moving end.

afterFigure.text: For the tap, f(t) = 2t and A(x) = x². At minute 3 the bath is gaining water at 6 litres per minute, which is the height of the rate graph there and also the slope of the running total. Integrating a rate and then differentiating the result bring you back to the rate. The two operations undo each other, and this is the second half of the fundamental theorem.

cases.label: Slope of the total at minute 3

lead.text: A running total grows at the rate at its moving end. Use that for a different rate.

reveal.text: You put x = 4 into the rate itself. The total built up so far is a different number, and its growth rate at that moment is the rate f(4).

lead.text: A(x) is the integral of t² + 1 from 0 to x. You do not need to integrate it. Ask how fast A is growing.

reveal.text: A′(x) was the rate itself, evaluated at the moving end. Integrating and differentiating undo each other.

lessons.orientation: Evaluate definite integrals with antiderivatives and differentiate accumulation functions.
